newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong handover venue springs a leak.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong handover venue springs a leak.

text.p: Officials faced embarrassing problems with a leak in the gigantic roof of Hong Kong's historic handover venue on Saturday but they promised to keep their VIP guests dry on the night that China takes over.

Workmen hurried to put finishing touches on the ceremonial venue of the handover to China, an immense convention centre jutting into the sea from the Wanchai red light district. Journalists given a sneak preview saw water dripping from the ceiling of the Grand Hall of the centre on Friday and Saturday after torrential rains fell on the British colony.
The water tumbled on to the spot where 4,000 VIPS including leaders from Britain, China and the United States will take part in the flag changing ceremony at midnight on June 30.
The venue was also set to host 2,800 of Hong Kong's rich and famous at a charity dinner to inaugurate the building on Saturday night.
Niels Kraunsoe, the centre's chief executive, said the leak was sheer bad luck as rain happened to bucket down as workmen serviced 200 pipes that drain the four hectare (10 acre) roof.

"As part of the commissioning system we had some of those pipes being checked yesterday, and when you have really heavy rain like that, we were just caught short at the unfortunate moment," Kraunsoe said.
He swore the problem was now fixed, although journalists saw water still dripping in some parts of the building only hours before the inagural banquet got under way.
"There's no contingency plan, it's not going to drip on the night, it's not going to drip tomorrow," he promised.

The striking, HK$4.8 billion (US$615 million) building shot up in a speedy 39 months on a man-made island on the Wanchai waterfront -- once known only for its girlie bars but now also home to many gleaming office towers and top-notch hotels.
"It is a vision of Hong Kong as Asia's pre-eminent city in international business," said Victor Fung, chairman of Hong Kong's Trade Development Council, describing the building's wing-shaped roof.
"It is much more than just a pretty face on the Wanchai waterfront," he said.

Hong Kong people had watched with enormous suspense in recent weeks and wondered if the building would be finished in time to host the handover, to be presided over by heir to the British throne Prince Charles and China's President Jiang Zemin.
Up until last month bamboo scaffolding -- the remnants of 450 kilometres (280 miles) of bamboo used in the project -- still covered much of the glass facade overlooking the harbour.
But the project was finished, aside from some cleaning and internal fitting out, Kraunsoe said.
The handover ceremony will take place on a specially constructed stage -- whose top-secret design is still veiled from sight -- in a Grand Foyer, with the harbour as backdrop.
The guests will be sitting in the Grand Hall, which normally faces the other way but whose seating arrangement was turned north toward the stage -- and Beijing -- for the ceremony.
Following the handover ceremony, almost everybody will walk to one of the exhibit halls where the new Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government will be sworn in.

Kraunsoe said moving 4,000 or so people could take up to 45 minutes -- ample time for those boycotting the inauguration of a controversial provisional legislature, such as U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and British Prime Minister Tony Blair, to duck out.
